Drastic Effect of Salt Concentration in Ionic Liquid on Performance of Lithium Sulfur Battery Yueying Peng,1,2 Rajashekar Badam,2 Tejkiran Pindi Jayakumar,2 Wannaruedee Wannapakdee,3 Chuchawin Changtong,3 and Noriyoshi Matsumi2,z 1Rechargeable Battery Materials Group, Centre for Green Research on Energy and Environmental Materials, National Institute for Materials Science, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-0044, Japan 2Graduate School of Advanced Science and Technology, Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology, Nomi, Ishikawa 923-1292, Japan 3IRPC Innovation Center, Chenong Nern, Rayong 21000, Thailand Lithium sulfur (Li–S) battery is an appealing energy storage system due to its high theoretical specific capacity and specific energy.
However, two main challenges, lithium polysulfides (LPS) dissolution from the sulfur cathode and the unstable Li anode, impede the practical application of Li–S battery.
Developing advanced electrolyte is an effective strategy to tune the stability of both sulfur cathode and Li anode.
Here, a concentrated imidazolium-based ionic liquids (IL) electrolyte was explored for Li–S battery with the synergistic advantages of both IL and high concentrated electrolyte.
A systematic study was conducted to reveal the effect of salt concentration on the properties of the IL electrolyte and the electrochemical performances of Li–S battery.
It is found that an effective suppression of LPS dissolution and improved stability of Li anode can be obtained with increase of salt concentration.
As a result, a good cycling stability of the Li–S battery is achieved in the concentrated IL electrolyte, with high capacity retention of 92% after 100 cycles at current density of 0.1 C.

The concentrated electrolyte based on IL solvent exhibits good compatibility with both cathode and anode, offering a new opportunity for designing electrolyte to achieve stable electrochemical system. © 2022 The Electrochemical Society (“ECS”).

Supplementary material for this article is available online Lithium sulfur (Li–S) battery, using sulfur as the cathode and Li metal as the anode, is regarded as one of the most promising candidates for next-generation energy storage system due to its high theoretical specific capacity (1675 mAh g−1) and high specific energy (2600 Wh kg−1).1,2 In addition, the elemental sulfur is naturally abundant, environmentally friendly and low cost.
Nevertheless, Li–S battery suffers from practical challenges of low active material utilization, poor cycle stability, low Coulombic efficiency and safety hazards.

These issues are mainly resulted from the incompatibility of electrolyte with both sulfur cathode and Li anode.3,4 On the side of sulfur cathode, the serious dissolution and shuttle of lithium polysulfides (LPS, Li2Sx, 2 < x ⩽8) is considered as the primary problem.

The LPS are generated as the reductive intermediates from the elemental sulfur that can be easily dissolved into organic electrolyte before forming into the final reductive products of Li2S/Li2S2, leading to the massive loss of active material and fast capacity fading.5 Besides, such dissolution phenomenon can even spontaneously occur during the static storage period, causing the open circuit voltage (OCV) fall and energy loss, which is so-called self-discharging behavior.6,7 In addition, the dissolved LPS can cross over the separator and migrate to the Li anode, where it reacts with Li to trigger shuttle effect, leading to poor Coulombic efficiency, irreversible capacity loss and Li anode corrosion.8 On the side of Li anode, the main problem is the instability of solid electrolyte interface (SEI), which is generated by the spontaneous reaction of Li anode with electrolyte.

Randomly formed SEI is usually not strong enough to bear the huge volume expansion during Li plating/ stripping processes, leading to repetitive fracture of SEI and continuous consumption of electrolyte, and even Li dendrite formation.9 Alongside, aforementioned LPS dissolution aggravates the corrosion of Li surface.

Various strategies have been worked out to improve the performances of Li–S cells, such as optimizing the electrolyte,10 fabricating sulfur cathodes11 and protecting Li anode.12 Among them, increasing the salt concentration to fabricate the concentrated electrolyte has been receiving intense attention due to its unique solvation structure to realize attractive functions, especially for suppressing LPS dissolution and stabilizing Li anode.13 For example, Chen’s group10 found that an improved capacity retention and Coulombic efficiency nearing 100% were achieved by simply increasing the salt concentration in typical electrolyte system (LiTFSI in 1,3-dioxolane (DOL) and 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME)), which was disclosed by the effective suppression of both LPS dissolution and Li dendrite growth.

The function of protecting Li has been largely demonstrated, which is revealed by the uniform Li deposition and dissolution in the concentrated electrolyte.14,15 Despite the attractive advantages of the concentrated electrolyte, several issues are still needed to be improved with regard to the solvents.

Traditional organic solvents, such as ethers and sulfones, are popularly adopted to design the electrolyte, posing the threat of LPS dissolution due to their intrinsic high affinity towards LPS.16 Besides, the hidden safety hazards still exist as most of these organic solvents are volatile and flammable.
Therefore, there is strong need to explore alternatives to replace the traditional organic solvents.
In this regard, ionic liquids (IL) might be promising alternatives due to their unique physicochemical properties.

Generally, IL show week interaction to LPS due to their weak Lewis acidic cations and Lewis basic anions, reducing the risk of LPS dissolution.17 Besides, IL are featured with the properties of low volatility, non-flammability, and large electrochemical stability, providing improved safety.18 Nevertheless, it is doubtful to combine the advantages of concentrated electrolyte and IL for Li–S battery.
The main concern is the high viscosity of general IL, resulting in slow ionic conductivity.
Increasing salt concentration usually results in higher viscosity,19 which might make this problem much worse.
Hence, low concentration (typically 0.5 ∼1 M) or mixture with other solvents are commonly employed in IL-based electrolyte.
Though there are several works employing IL electrolyte with relatively high salt concentration,20,21 their research for Li–S battery is very limited.
To explore the feasibility of using concentrated IL electrolyte for Li–S battery, a relatively high salt concentration is urgently needed.

Bearing these in mind, we try to prepare concentrated electrolyte by using IL as the solvent and explore its influence on the electrochemical performances of Li–S battery.

By using 1-Allyl-3- methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (AMImTFSI) as the solvent and lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI) as the salt, a concentrated IL electrolyte with relatively high salt concentration of 3 M was achieved.
The properties of the electrolyte containing different salt concentration were measured for better understanding its influence on the electrochemical performances of Li–S battery.

To evaluate its compatibility with both electrodes, the effects of the IL electrolyte on both sulfur cathode and Li anode were systematically studied in terms of the electrode morphologies, chemical components, and interfacial properties.
Our study offers a new alternative way to design electrolyte for Li–S batteries with stable cathode and anode.

Experimental Materials and regents.—Ketjen Black (KB, EC660-JD, Lion Specialty Chemicals Corporation, ash content 0.1%), sulfur (Sigma- Aldrich, 99.98%), lithium sulfide (Li2S, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.98%), lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (LiTFSI, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.95%), 1-allyl-3-methylimidazolium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (AMImTFSI, Tokyo Chemical Industry (TCI), > 98%), acetylene black (AB, Denka, ash content 0.01%), Sodium Carboxymethyl Cellulose (CMC, Sigma-Aldrich, average Mw ∼250,000), Styrene-butadiene rubber (SBR, NIPPON A&L INC.), dimethoxyethane (DME, Sigma-Aldrich, 99.5%).

Sample preparation.—Three types of electrolytes were prepared with LiTFSI concentration of 1 M, 2 M and 3 M, which are denoted as 1 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, 2 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, and 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, respectively.
Conventionally used sulfur/KB (S/KB) composite was utilized to evaluate the performance of as prepared electrolytes.
Sulfur and KB was mixed with mass ratio of 3:2, followed by heating at 155 °C for 12 h in a tube furnace under inert atmosphere.
Lithium polysulfides (LPS) dissolution experiment.—LPS was synthesized to directly observe its dissolution in the electrolytes prepared.
Herein, Li2S4 was synthesized as a typical representative of LPS.

Based on the reaction of Li S Li S 8 S x 1 8 , x 2 8 2 + ( − ) → 16 0.4 M Li2S4 was synthesized by taking stoichiometric amount of Li2S and sulfur with a molar ratio of 8:3 in a vial containing 1 ml electrolyte.
Then, the mixture was stirred and heated at 80 °C for 50 h and thereafter maintained at 30 °C for 48 h with stirring.
All the above procedure was performed under inert atmosphere.
Characterization and calculation.—The viscosity was measured by viscometer (TV-35, TOKI SANGYO) equipped with a thermostat.

The ionic conductivity was analyzed by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) technique in the frequency range from 1 MHz to 10 mHz with voltage amplitude of 10 mV and temperature range of 30 °C∼60 °C using an impedance analyzer (Solartron 1260).
The morphologies of electrodes were observed by scanning electronic microscopy (SEM, S-4500, Hitachi).
Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) and elemental mapping was also collected by SEM (TM3030Plus tabletop microscope, Hitachi).
Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was performed on S-probe TM 2803, Fisons Instruments.
The cycled cells were disassembled and washed by enough DME in Ar-filled glove box, followed by dried under vacuum overnight before SEM and XPS characterization.
The geometric optimization and electronic properties were evaluated based on density functional theory (DFT) calculations using Gaussian 16 software.
Calculations were performed on a B3LYP functional equipped with a 6-311 G(d,p) basis set.
The increased concentrated condition was simulated by increasing the number of anions around IL.

Cell fabrication and electrochemical measurements.—The slurry for sulfur electrode was prepared by mixing S/KB, AB and CMC/SBR (1:1 wt/wt) with a mass ratio of 70:20:10 in deionized water as solvent using planetary centrifugal mixer (Kakuhunter SK- 350TII).
The slurry was coated on aluminum foil (15 μm thick) using doctor blade.
After drying at 60 °C in vacuum oven overnight, the electrodes were punched into circular disks with 15 mm diameter.
The obtained sulfur mass loading in this work was ∼1 mg cm−2.
The fabricated S/KB electrode was used as cathode.
Circular disk of Li foil with 15 mm diameter was used as both reference and counter electrode.
Using the as prepared electrolyte, the electrochemical performance was evaluated in CR2025-type coin cell configuration.
Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was performed with electrochemical workstation (Bio-Logic VSP) with a scanning rate of 0.05 mV s−1 in the voltage range of 1.6∼2.8 V vs Li/Li+.

The cycling stability and discharge/charge plots were evaluated using galvanostatic charge discharge technique at the current density of 0.05 C (1 C = 1.672 mA g−1) within the potential range of 1.6∼2.8 V vs Li/Li+.

Results and Discussion The properties of the electrolyte.—Considering that the physicochemical properties of the electrolyte have a closed relationship with the electrochemical performances, the effect of salt concentration on the properties of the fabricated electrolyte were studied.
Firstly, the viscosity (η), reflecting the liquidity and ionic mobility, was measured, as shown in Fig. 1a.

The effect of temperature on the viscosity of AMImTFSI-based electrolyte was analyzed by classical Arrhenius-type equation.22,23 ⎛ ⎝ ⎞ ⎠ E RT exp 1 a η η = − [ ] ∞ where η∞is the viscosity at infinite temperature, Ea is the activation energy and R is the universal gas constant.

When plotting the viscosity (log η) as a function of temperature (1000/T) in Fig. 1b, very good straight lines can be obtained in all tested electrolyte, indicating no phase change happens during the measured temperature range of 25∼60 °C.
The viscosity of the electrolyte is found to be increasing as increasing the salt concentration.
For example, the values of viscosity at 298 K for pure AMImTFSI, 1 M LiTFSI, 2 M LiTFSI and 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI are 30.1, 76.0, 236.4 and 664.0 mPa·s, respectively.

Thus, the ionic conductivities of the fabricated electrolyte were estimated in Fig. 1c.
The values of ionic conductivity with acceptable order of magnitude of 10−3 S·cm−1 are exhibited in all cases of electrolyte.
Among them, the highest ionic conductivity is found in the low concentration electrolyte with 1 M LiTFSI, while very close values are observed in the case of 2 M and 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI.

Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann (VFT) approach, with modified version of Arrhenius equation, was employed to understand the ionic conductivity-temperature dependence for IL.27,28 ⎡ ⎣⎢ ⎤ ⎦⎥ AT B T T exp 4 0.5 0 σ = − − [ ] where T0 is the “ideal glass transition temperature,” A and B are the factors related to the carrier ion number and activation energy for ion transport, respectively.
As shown in Fig. 1d, the profiles of ln(σT−0.5) vs 1000/T exhibit good VFT behavior with linear feature.
The fitted parameters from VFT equation are listed in Table SI.

It is found that the values of A and B display decreased tendency with increased salt concentration, suggesting decreased carrier ion number and activation energy.27 This gives good reason for the lower ionic conductivity in the electrolyte with higher salt concentration.
In a dilute electrolyte, the solvent-separated ions are predominant.
Thus, increasing salt concentration can generate more charge carriers.

While, in the concentrated electrolyte, the associated salt molecules are dominant and thereby increased salt cannot contribute to the free mobile ions.13 To further evaluate the effect of salt concentration on LPS dissolution, LPS dissolution experiment was conducted to directly observe the LPS formation from the visible color change.
As shown in Fig. 1e obvious red color is found in the cases of 1 M and 2 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, reflecting the large amount of LPS formation.
While, very less color change is detected for 3 M LiTFSI in Figure 1.

Corresponding UV–vis spectra were further collected in Fig. 1f, confirming the absence of LPS peaks for 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI.

It should be note that this result is achieved by using 3 M salt in IL, which is lower than the values needed in traditional organic solvent (typically > 4 M), displaying the superiority of IL in terms of suppressing LPS dissolution.

From the above results, it can be concluded that increasing salt concentration can effectively suppress LPS dissolution and diffusion into the electrolyte benefited from the increased viscosity, decreased diffusion, and common ionic effect.
Thereby, Li–S battery is expected to show decreased active material loss and improved cycling stability.

Even though, lower mobility of the carrier ions and decreased carrier ion number are observed with the increase of salt concentration, resulting in decreased ionic conductivity, which might affect the ionic transportation.

The electrochemical performances of Li–S battery.—To remove the ambiguity regarding performance contribution from other components of the battery, conventional cathode material, sulfur/ Ketjen Black (S/KB) composite containing sulfur weight amount of 60% without any modification (Fig.
S1 (available online at stacks. iop.org/JES/169/050515/mmedia)), and the electrolyte with LiTFSI as the salt and AMImTFSI as the solvent were used without any additives.
In such simple system, the sole effect of the electrolyte on the electrochemical performances can directly be observed.
Considering the problem of self-discharge induced by LPS dissolution, the changes in the OCV of Li–S battery were monitored after the cell fabrication without applying current.
As shown in Fig. 2a, the OCV for Li–S cell of 1 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI gradually decreases from initial 2.88 V to 2.67 V, with potential retention of 92.7% after 30 d.
In contrast, 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI as electrolyte holds higher potential retention of 96.8% after 30 d.

From the comparison of specific values in Table SII, the change of OCV clearly decreased with increased LiTFSI concentration, indicating that increasing salt concentration in IL electrolyte can help suppress self-discharge effect, which is consistent with the results of viscosity and LPS dissolution measurements.
Figure 2b compares the cycling performance of Li–S battery in the fabricated IL electrolyte at the current density of 0.05 C (1 C = 1.672 mA g−1) with potential window of 1.6 ∼2.8 V.
For 1 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, the capacity shows the lowest value with a fast fading and fluctuant Coulombic efficiency.
Improved capacity and cycling stability can be seen when increasing salt concentration.
The electrolyte of 2 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI exhibits the highest initial capacity, while a fast capacity fading is still observed.
Though a moderate initial capacity of 1071 mAh g−1 is obtained in 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI as electrolyte, a good cyclability with stable capacity of ∼950 mAh g−1 can be achieved during the 50 cycles.
The cycling performance of 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI as electrolyte was further assessed at higher current density of 0.1 C in Fig. 2c.
Still, a very good cycling stability can be obtained, with capacity retention of 92% after 100 cycles.
From the results of OCV, viscosity and LPS dissolution experiment, the enhanced cycling stability in 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI can be attributed to the effective suppression of LPS.
The moderate value of initial capacity might be caused by the increased viscosity and decreased ionic conductivity, reducing the reactive kinetics.
This speculation can be further supported from the corresponding discharge/charge plots in Figs. 2d–2f.
For 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, the largest voltage hysteresis of 0.51 V is found, indicating the large polarization and reduced redox kinetics.
While, a highly overlapping discharge/ charge curves is displayed, reflective of the stable electrochemical reaction.
From the above results, it can be concluded that increasing salt concentration likes a double-edged sword for the electrochemical performances of Li–S battery.

One the one hand, decreased selfdischarge, improved cycling stability and Coulombic efficiency can be achieved, attributing to the effective suppression of LPS dissolution in the concentrated IL electrolyte.
One the other hand, decreased initial capacity is obtained as the increased polarization.
It should make a balance between the cyclability and capacity when increasing the salt concentration.

The effects of electrolyte on the sulfur cathode.—To reveal the fundamental mechanism for the electrochemical behaviors, the influence of the concentrated IL electrolyte on both cathode and anode were investigated.
Firstly, theoretical study based on density functional theory (DFT) was conducted to understand the reactivity of electrolyte under different salt concentration.
The results were analyzed to evaluate the electronic configuration of the electrolyte systems.

With increasing salt concentration, an upshift in the energy level for the electrolyte system is observed.
The higher EHOMO reflects an easier removal of an electron from the orbital, suggesting a higher possibility of oxidation on the cathode enabling the formation of a protecting film on cathode.
While the higher ELUMO stands for the accepting electron ability becomes more difficult, indicating more difficult reduction on the anode.

From the comparison of surface and cross-sectional SEM images, such surface film becomes more obvious and denser as salt concentration increases, indicating that increasing salt concentration can facilitate the formation of surface film.

This will be another added feature that contributes to higher OCV retention and increased cycle performance with the increase of salt concentration.
To further reveal the chemical composition of the surface film on the cathode, XPS measurements were conducted for the electrodes after 50 cycles.
The batteries were at charged-statement of 2.8 V before disassembling for XPS studies.
Figure 4a–4f compares the high-resolution S 2p, C 1s, F 1s, Li 1s, and N 1s XPS spectra and corresponding atomic concentration ratio of C–F and Li–F.

Careful deconvoluting S 2p XPS spectra in Fig. 4a, typical polysulfides species with a doublet of peaks for terminal sulfur (ST 1−) at 161.9 eV and bridging sulfur (SB 0) at 163.8 eV can be observed in all cases.32,33 The terminal and bridging sulfur moieties are resulted from the electrochemical reaction of sulfur cathode during charging (Li2S/Li2S2 →Li2Sx).

Besides, a broad peak at 166.0 eV (-SxOy) and a strong peak at 169.5 eV (R–SO2–R) can be obtained in all cases, which is associated with TFSI anion decomposition.34 Such observation indicates that additional reaction from TFSI anion might happen on the sulfur cathode.
This hypothesis can be proved by the deconvolution of C 1s XPS spectra in Fig. 4b.

In the lower binding energy religion of C 1s, four peaks of 284.5 eV (Caliphalic, C–C/ C–H), 285.5 eV (Chetero, C6/C7), 287.0 eV (Cinter,C4/C5), and 288.8 eV (C2) originated from Ccation in the AMIm cation group are observed,35 implying that AMIm cation also participates in the surface film formation.

With increasing the LiTFSI concentration, two peaks located at 290.5 eV and 293.4 eV become stronger, which can be ascribed to C–SO2 and C–F3, respectively.36 This indicates that the TFSI anion decomposition becomes easier with increasing salt concentration, which is well agreed with the DFT calculations suggesting presence of higher EHOMO in the higher concentration electrolyte.
The TFSI anion decomposition can also be supported by the F 1s and Li 1s XPS spectra.

From the Li 1s XPS spectra in Fig. 4d, the peaks associated the inorganic components of LiF, LixSOy, Li3N and Li2O can be detected, which can be ascribed to the decomposed products from TFSI anion.37 From the F 1s XPS spectra in Fig. 4c, two clear peaks associated with C–F (C–Fx) and Li–F (LiF) bond are exhibited.

In addition, the percentage of Li–F shows an increasing tendency with increased LiTFSI concentration in Fig. 4f, which is believed to be good for building a stable SEI due to its high electrochemical stability to suppress the side reaction at the electrode/electrolyte interface.38 The aforementioned reactions of TFSI anion and AMIm cation can also be demonstrated from N 1s spectra, in which the peak at 400.0 eV corresponding to TFSI anion (denoted as Nanion) and the peak at 402.1 eV corresponding to AMIm cation (denoted as Ncation) can be clearly detected.39 On the basis of literatures8 and results of XPS spectra, the cathode surface film formation mechanism in the concentrated IL electrolyte can be proposed in the following manner.
Firstly, the TFSI anion is decomposed by breaking of C–S or S–N bond to produce molecular groups like R–SO2–R, –CFx, and further decomposed to small fragments, like LiF, LixSOy, and Li–N.

Furthermore, the decomposition of TFSI anion would induce the AMIm cation polymerization on the cathode based on the following reaction.40 From the above results, it can be concluded that the AMImTFSIbased electrolyte with concentrated LiTFSI is helpful to decrease the polysulfide dissolution through two effect.
One is the formation of surface film on the sulfur cathode, which is generated by the TFSI anion decomposition and AMIm cation polymerization in the concentrated AMImTFSI-based electrolyte.
The formed surface film can act as a protective film to suppress the LPS diffusion into the electrolyte.
Another is the increased viscosity and ionic effect make it difficult for LPS to dissolve and diffuse in the concentrated IL electrolyte.
As a result, improved cycling stability can be achieved in the concentrated AMImTFSI-based IL electrolyte.
The effects of electrolyte on the Li anode.—Furthermore, the effects of the electrolyte on the Li anode was investigated.
Firstly, the surface and cross-section SEM images of the Li anode after 50 cycles were observed in Figs. 5a–5c.
For the 1 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, a rough surface and loose cross-section images with visibly mossy Li is found, which could be due to the inhomogeneous Li plating/striping processes.
With the increase of LiTFSI concentration, the surface morphologies of Li anode become smoother and Figure 4.

The SEI components on the anode were further analyzed by XPS spectra in Figs. 5d–5f.

From the S 2p XPS spectra (Fig. 5d), the peaks associated with polysulfides species (located 160 ∼165 eV) is only found in 1 M LiTFSI, while no corresponding peaks are found in the cases of 2 M and 3 M LiTFSI.
This indicates that LPS shuttle effect can be effectively suppressed by increasing salt concentration.
In the higher binding energy regions, all three cases exhibit the peaks associated with TFSI anion decomposed products (–SOxOy and R–SO2–R).
Similar with the XPS analysis for the cathode, the TFSI anion decomposition and AMIm cation polymerization can also be seen from the C 1s, Li 1s and N 1s XPS spectra (Figs.
In addition, the content of Li–F is increased with increased LiTFSI concentration in Fig. 5f.

It is largely demonstrated that LiF-rich SEI can help to improve the uniformity and stability of the Li anode,41,42 which gives a good reason for the uniform and dense SEM surface images of Li anode as observed in the case of 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI.
To evaluate the durability of the SEI on the Li anode, the cycled cells were disassembled, and exposed to air (Fig.
Compared with the traditional electrolyte (1 M LiTFSI in DOL:DME with 1% LiNO3), much clear Li metal surfaces are observed in AMImTFSIbased electrolytes.
Especially in the case of 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, a relatively shinier surface is still maintained after 20 min of exposure to ambient air.
Furthermore, symmetric Li–Li cells were fabricated and their impedance were monitored to evaluate the stability of the SEI for over 30 d.
Before the EIS measurements, the symmetric Li–Li cells experience the process of Li deposition/dissolution at 0.1 mA cm−2 with a fix areal capacity of 1 mAh cm−2 for one cycle to form SEI.
The collected Nyquist plots and fitted data are illustrated in Fig.
For 1 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI, the resistance is found to be fluctuated during the 30 d monitor, indicating an unstable Li/electrolyte interface.
With the increase of salt concentration, much stable values of resistance are obtained.
This suggests that the formed SEI on the Li surface is much more stable in the higher salt concentration electrolyte.
Conclusions In summary, a concentrated IL electrolyte was explored for Li–S battery with the synergistic advantages of both IL and high concentrated electrolyte.

IL electrolyte and the electrochemical performances of Li–S batteries.
It is found that the concentrated IL electrolyte exhibits good compatibility with both sulfur cathode and Li anode.
For the sulfur cathode, an effective suppression of LPS dissolution is achieved because of the increased viscosity and the protective surface film formation on the cathode.
For the Li anode, a more uniform, dense, and durable SEI is observed, providing a stable Li anode.
As a result, Li–S cell exhibits a decreased self-discharge behavior, improved cyclability and Coulombic efficiency in the electrolyte of 3 M LiTFSI in AMImTFSI.

The concentrated IL electrolyte exhibits effective ability of suppressing LPS dissolution and protecting Li anode, offering an attractive strategy to design advanced electrolyte for high performance energy storage system.
